title: Circularity of biomedical polymeric materials: current state, challenges and a circularity readiness framework
content: The widespread use of polymeric materials in healthcare has generated a growing and increasingly complex waste stream, encompassing conventional thermoplastics, degradable and bioresorbable polymers, hydrogels, conductive polymers, and multifunctional polymer composites. Although these materials offer essential clinical functions, their circularity is constrained by contamination, sterilization, additives, multi-material architectures, clinical performance requirements, and regulatory considerations. Consequently, polymer recyclability alone does not necessarily translate into practical circularity. This review critically examines the current state of circularity for biomedical polymeric materials, linking material characteristics and biomedical applications with waste generation, contamination and decontamination, recovery technologies, environmental performance, and system-level implementation. This review compares mechanical recycling, solvent-based recovery, chemical depolymerization, biological conversion, and thermochemical treatment in terms of material-value retention, feedstock requirements, technological maturity, and sustainability considerations. Building on these insights, a Circularity Readiness Framework (CRF) is proposed comprising eight dimensions: material circularity, clinical and functional compatibility, contamination and decontamination readiness, design for recovery, end-of-life technology readiness, environmental performance, economic feasibility, and regulatory and traceability readiness. A preliminary Circularity Readiness Score (CRS) is further proposed as a screening tool to distinguish materials that are theoretically recyclable from biomedical polymer systems that are practically prepared for circular implementation. The review further highlights source segregation, validated decontamination, design-for-recovery, digital traceability, and integrated life-cycle assessment as critical enablers of circular healthcare systems. Future research should focus on standardized polymer-specific material-flow data, real-world recycling demonstrations, advanced chemical and biological recovery, digital biomedical polymer passports, and validation of circularity-readiness metrics. Overall, the transition from linear biomedical polymer use towards circular systems requires a shift from end-of-life recycling to circularity-by-design, in which clinical functionality, material recovery, and environmental sustainability are considered simultaneously.
